vignette:
# Maria

Maria sits with her hands folded in her lap, her posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. At sixty-six, she carries herself with the disciplined bearing of someone who has spent four decades in security work—first as a guard at a hospital, later at a corporate office downtown. Her dark eyes, framed by wire-rimmed glasses, seem to look through rather than at the world around her.

Her husband, Rajesh, suffered a severe stroke three years ago. Maria was at work when the call came—a neighbor had found him on the kitchen floor that morning, confused and unable to move his right side. She remembers the exact time: 10:47 a.m. She remembers the fluorescent lights of the hospital corridor, the smell of antiseptic, the neurologist's careful explanation of what had happened in Rajesh's brain. She remembers standing in the doorway of his ICU room, watching his mouth struggle to form words that wouldn't come.

For the first months after his discharge, Maria took a leave from work. She became his primary caregiver, learning to help him dress, managing his medications, attending physical therapy appointments. But something shifted inside her during those early weeks—a hypervigilance that wouldn't settle. She found herself checking on Rajesh compulsively throughout the night, sometimes every fifteen minutes, afraid that another stroke would happen while she slept. She'd wake gasping from dreams where she couldn't reach him, where the phone rang but she couldn't answer it in time.

When she returned to work after four months, the anxiety intensified rather than improved. At the security desk, her mind would drift to catastrophic scenarios. What if Rajesh fell while she was away? What if he had another stroke and couldn't call for help? She'd find herself calling home repeatedly, asking her daughter—who visited daily—to check on him. Her daughter eventually stopped answering, which sent Maria into spirals of panic at work.

The sounds of the office became unbearable. The sudden ring of the phone made her chest tighten. A coworker collapsing during their lunch break—nothing serious, just low blood sugar—triggered a full panic attack that left Maria shaking for hours. She couldn't watch medical shows anymore. She'd change the channel instantly if any health emergency appeared, her heart racing as if she were back in that hospital corridor.

Now, three years later, Maria still works security, but her world has contracted. She avoids driving past hospitals. She's stopped attending family gatherings because the drive feels too risky, and she's convinced something will happen at home while she's away. She sleeps poorly, usually only three or four hours, her sleep fragmented by nightmares where Rajesh is calling for help and she can't reach him. She wakes with her heart pounding, sometimes unsure for a moment whether the dream was real.

Her relationship with Rajesh has become strained in ways she struggles to articulate. She loves him fiercely, but she also resents him—resents the stroke, resents the way her life now orbits around preventing another one, resents that her fear has made her irritable with him. She feels guilty for these feelings, which only deepens her anxiety.

At work, her colleagues have noticed the change. She's more withdrawn, more easily startled. She's called in sick more often. The job that once gave her a sense of purpose—protecting the building and its people—now feels suffocating. She watches the security monitors and sees danger everywhere. She understands, intellectually, that she cannot prevent tragedy. But her nervous system has not received this message.
